posts.title: A Summer on the Data Flywheel
posts.excerpt: Notes from a summer internship on Microsoft's Data Flywheel team: building an LLM-powered bug triage system for Word, restarting a project six weeks in, and learning where to draw the line between model judgment and deterministic code.
posts.content:
I spent May through August 2026 in Redmond as a software engineering intern on Microsoft's Data Flywheel team. The nominal assignment was to build an LLM-powered bug triage system for Word. What I actually got was a lesson in how reliability work happens at the scale of a product with hundreds of millions of users — and a lesson in what to do when the first version of your project turns out to be the wrong version.

Here's how it went, roughly in order.

May: the wrong problem

The first stretch was misaligned. I was building toward a problem framing that didn't match what the team needed, and by the time that became clear, the project had to be restarted more or less from the top. That's an uncomfortable place to be six weeks into a twelve-week internship. It's also, I'd argue, the single most useful thing that happened all summer, because everything after it was shaped by having gotten it wrong once.

The correction was mostly about scope. I had been thinking of the system as something I would design; the useful version was something that would extend infrastructure the team already ran. Microsoft has a standardized Reliability AI agent, and the right move was to build onto it rather than around it.

June: telemetry and the shape of the data

Word's crash telemetry arrives through Kusto and OpenTelemetry. Before anything intelligent can be layered on top, you have to understand what a "crash spike" actually is in that data — how noisy the signal is, how spikes cluster, how much of the volume is a handful of recurring failure modes versus a long tail.

The eventual system evaluated over 100,000 Word Copilot crash spikes, running on Azure DevOps and SQL. The bulk of the early work was less glamorous than that number suggests: figuring out what to feed the model, what to compute deterministically, and how to tell the difference.

July: LLM judgment vs. deterministic heuristics

This was the real design question, and it's the thing I'd want to talk about if you asked me about the internship at a bar.

An automated triage system has to make a series of calls: is this spike the same as that one, what component is at fault, what's the likely root cause, how urgent is it. Some of those are pattern-matching problems where an LLM is straightforwardly better than a rules engine. Others are the kind of thing where a heuristic is not only sufficient but preferable, because it's stable, auditable, and doesn't quietly change behavior when the model does.

The instinct when you've been handed an LLM is to route everything through it. That instinct is wrong. A lot of my July was spent pulling decisions back out of the model and into deterministic code, and keeping the model where genuine ambiguity lived.

The same reasoning drove the biggest product decision: the system does not auto-assign bugs. It produces root-cause summaries and a ranked queue that humans work through. Auto-assignment is a much flashier demo, and it's also the version where a confident wrong answer costs an engineer half a day. Ranked queue plus summary keeps the model in an advisory role, where being 85% right is genuinely useful instead of actively harmful.

I also built daily reporting into the agent, so triage state was continuously visible rather than something you had to go pull.

Throughout: actually shipping fixes

Running in parallel to the triage system, I shipped fixes for critical Word bugs, collectively eliminating 50,000+ enterprise-facing crashes. This is the part of the summer I'd point to if someone wanted a single number, though it's worth being honest that finding these was often easier than fixing them — the telemetry work and the fix work fed each other.

I also spent time with the NLX team on Word's proof checker (the spell and grammar checker). There was a bug in how multi-word expressions were handled that produced visible nonsense in user-facing suggestions. The fix was a filter at the suggestion layer rather than deeper in the pipeline — a smaller, safer intervention that removed the bad output without disturbing anything upstream. Validation included a Hungarian-language audit, which was a nice excuse to use a language I actually speak in a place where it mattered.

August: the unsanctioned version

With about a week left, I had a working solution and a nagging feeling that it was the slow, manual version of a problem that admitted a better answer. So I built the better answer on my own time, tested it, and got a promising early result.

I don't want to oversell this — an early result on a one-week build is an early result, not a shipped system. But it clarified something for me about how to work inside a large organization. The version of me that started in May would have either kept quiet about it or presented it as a repudiation of the sanctioned approach. Neither is right. The useful framing is: here is the thing we agreed on, it works, and here is a direction I think is worth someone's time after I leave.

What I'd take away

Three things, if I'm being concise about it:

Being wrong early is cheap; being wrong late is expensive. The restart hurt, but it happened while there was still runway.

"Use an LLM" is not a design. The interesting work is drawing the line between what the model decides and what your code decides, and defending that line.

Extend before you invent. The most useful thing I built was an extension of infrastructure that already existed and that people already trusted. That's not a compromise; that's the job.

Thanks to the Data Flywheel and NLX teams for the summer.

posts.title: Welcome to My Blog
posts.excerpt: Starting a blog to share updates on projects, learning experiences, and other interesting things I'm working on.
posts.content:
Welcome to my blog! I'm starting this as a way to document my journey in computer science, machine learning, and software engineering.

Here I'll share updates on projects I'm working on, things I'm learning, and other interesting developments in my work and studies.

Stay tuned for more posts!
